Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit, let $\delta\in R$, and let $n\ge0$. Let $t$ be an integer with $0\le t\le n$ and $n-t$ even. The diagram module $M_R(n,t)$ has $n$ bottom boundary points and $t$ top boundary points, with stacking and loop removal as in [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]]. A component of a basis diagram is **propagating** if it meets both the bottom and top boundaries. Write $\operatorname{prop}(D)$ for the number of propagating components of a diagram $D:n\to t$.

Let $M_R^{<t}(n,t)$ be the $R$-span of the basis diagrams $D:n\to t$ with $\operatorname{prop}(D)<t$. Define the **Temperley–Lieb link-state standard module**

$$W_{n,t}(R,\delta):=M_R(n,t)/M_R^{<t}(n,t).$$

Write $T_{n,t}$ for the set of diagrams in $\mathcal D(n,t)$ with exactly $t$ propagating components. The cosets of these diagrams form an $R$-basis of $W_{n,t}$. Identifying each diagram with its bottom arcs and defects gives a partial matching of the $n$ ordered bottom sites, with the additional condition that the $t$ unpaired sites are joined to the ordered top sites by noncrossing propagating strands. In particular, no defect lies inside an arc. The unpaired sites are called **defects**. Thus $t$ is the defect or through-line number; in sources using $p$ for the number of arcs, $p=(n-t)/2$.

The intended right action of $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ is $x\cdot a=[x\circ a]$, where $x\in M_R(n,t)$, $a\in M_R(n,n)$, and $x\circ a$ stacks $x$ above $a$. The submodule $M_R^{<t}(n,t)$ is stable under this action, so it descends to $W_{n,t}$; the complete well-definedness argument is [[lem-temperley-lieb-link-state-module-action-is-well-defined]].

Let $n\ge0$ and let $t$ satisfy $0\le t\le n$ and $n-t$ even. Put $a=(n-t)/2$, the number of arcs in a link state, and use the convention $\binom{n}{a-1}=0$ when $a=0$. Then the link-state basis $T_{n,t}$ of $W_{n,t}(R,\delta)$ has cardinality

$$|T_{n,t}|=\binom{n}{a}-\binom{n}{a-1}.$$

In particular, $W_{n,t}$ is free of this rank over $R$, independently of $\delta$.

Let $R$, $\delta$, $n$, $t$ and $W_{n,t}(R,\delta)$ be as in [[def-temperley-lieb-link-state-standard-modules]]. For link states $x,y$, let $x^*$ denote reflection across a horizontal line. The diagram $y\circ x^*:t\to t$ is either $\delta^c1_t$ for some $c\ge0$ or has fewer than $t$ propagating components. Define $\phi_{n,t}(x,y)=\delta^c$ in the first case and $0$ in the second, and extend $R$-bilinearly. Then $\phi_{n,t}$ is symmetric and satisfies

$$\phi_{n,t}(x\cdot a,y)=\phi_{n,t}(x,y\cdot a^*)$$

for all $x,y\in W_{n,t}(R,\delta)$ and $a\in\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$. Here $a^*$ is reflection across a horizontal line. The matrix of $\phi_{n,t}$ in the link-state basis is the Gram matrix obtained by reflecting and capping two link states, with one factor $\delta$ for each closed loop.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit, $\delta\in R$, $n\ge1$, and let $t$ be allowed for $W_{n,t}(R,\delta)$. Include $\mathrm{TL}_{n-1}(R,\delta)$ into $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ by adding a rightmost vertical strand, and restrict the right action along this inclusion. Set $W_{m,s}=0$ when $s<0$, $s>m$, or $m-s$ is odd. Then there is a short exact sequence of right $\mathrm{TL}_{n-1}(R,\delta)$-modules

$$0\longrightarrow W_{n-1,t-1}\longrightarrow \operatorname{Res}^{TL_n}_{TL_{n-1}}W_{n,t}\longrightarrow W_{n-1,t+1}\longrightarrow0.$$

The sequence gives a two-step filtration; it is not asserted to split.

Let $F$ be a field, $\delta\in F$, and $n\ge0$. Put $D_{n,t}=W_{n,t}(F,\delta)/\operatorname{rad}(\phi_{n,t})$ for each allowed $t$. Then the nonzero $D_{n,t}$ are absolutely simple and form a complete set of pairwise nonisomorphic simple right $\mathrm{TL}_n(F,\delta)$-modules. Moreover, $D_{n,t}\ne0$ exactly when $\phi_{n,t}$ is not identically zero; in that case $\operatorname{rad}(\phi_{n,t})$ is the unique maximal proper submodule and $D_{n,t}$ is the simple head of $W_{n,t}$. If $\phi_{n,t}$ is identically zero, then $D_{n,t}=0$, but no conclusion about the actual head of $W_{n,t}$ follows.
A nonzero homomorphism between simple modules is an isomorphism. Consequently the endomorphism ring of a simple module is a division ring. See [[def-simple-module]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit and $\delta\in R$. Define the quantum integers by

$$[0]_\delta=0,\qquad [1]_\delta=1,\qquad [r+1]_\delta=\delta[r]_\delta-[r-1]_\delta\quad(r\ge1).$$

The **quantum characteristic** of $(R,\delta)$ is the least positive integer $\ell$ with $[\ell]_\delta=0$, if one exists, and $\ell=\infty$ otherwise. No element of $R$ is inverted in this definition.

For $q\in\mathbb C^\times$ and $\delta=q+q^{-1}$, write $[r]_q=[r]_\delta$. If $q\ne\pm1$, this agrees with $(q^r-q^{-r})/(q-q^{-1})$; at $q=\pm1$ the recurrence gives $[r]_q=rq^{r-1}$. For complex-parameter classification, write $\kappa=\operatorname{ord}(q^2)$, with $\kappa=\infty$ when $q^2$ has infinite order. If $q\ne\pm1$, the quantum characteristic equals $\kappa$ when $\kappa<\infty$ and is $\infty$ otherwise. At $q=\pm1$, $\kappa=1$ but the complex quantum characteristic is $\infty$, because $[r]_q=rq^{r-1}\ne0$ for every positive $r$.

For a field $K$ of positive characteristic $p$, set $p(0)=1$ and, when $\ell<\infty$, set $p(i)=\ell p^{i-1}$ for $i\ge1$. In characteristic zero and finite $\ell$, the finite digit scale is $p(1)=\ell$; the separate characteristic-zero criterion below uses $a\ell-1$ for arbitrary positive integers $a$. If $\ell=\infty$, every finite index is already in the range $n<\ell$.

derivations.claim: For $n=0$ and $n=1$, the only allowed arc count is $p=0$; the all-defect link state has Gram matrix $(1)$, agreeing with the empty product.

For any $n$, the $p=0$ module is spanned by the all-defect state and its form value is $1$. Now fix $n\ge2$ and assume inductively that the determinant formula holds at all smaller ranks; because no positive quantum integer vanishes when $q^2$ is not a root of unity, those smaller Gram forms are nondegenerate.

Suppose $n>2p>0$. By [F2], restriction has the rightmost-defect submodule $U\cong W_{n-1,n-1-2p}$ and quotient $W_{n-1,n-1-2(p-1)}$. Deleting the rightmost defect preserves the reflected-and-capped matching graph and its loop count, so the restricted form on $U$ is exactly the standard form with matrix $G_{n-1,p}$; it is nondegenerate by induction. Invariance [F1] makes $U^\perp$ invariant, and nondegeneracy on $U$ gives $W_{n,n-2p}=U\oplus U^\perp$. The quotient map identifies $U^\perp$ with the quotient module. The quotient's standard form is nondegenerate by induction, so [F3] makes it absolutely simple and the form identifies it with its dual. The form induced from $U^\perp$ is invariant; by [F4], its map to the dual is a scalar multiple of the standard form's map, say $\alpha_{n,p}$ times that map. Subtracting the submodule projection from each quotient lift is a block-triangular basis change with identity diagonal, so the Gram matrix in this basis is $G_{n-1,p}\oplus\alpha_{n,p}G_{n-1,p-1}$ and the change-of-basis determinant is $1$.

If $n=2p$ with $p>0$, deleting the rightmost endpoint and turning its partner into a defect bijects the link-state basis with that of $W_{2p-1,p-1}$. In the glued matching graph, the reduced pairing has one open path between the new defect ends; restoring the two terminal arcs closes exactly that path into one additional component and leaves every other component unchanged. Hence $G_{2p,p}=\delta G_{2p-1,p-1}$, which is the boundary scalar $\alpha_{2p,p}=\delta$.

For $n>2p$, refine the ordered link states into four types: type 1 has $n$ and $n-1$ both defects; type 2 has $n$ a defect and $n-1$ on an earlier arc; type 3 joins $n-1$ to $n$; and type 4 has $n$ on an arc whose partner is earlier than $n-1$. The gluing rule gives $G^{12}_{n,p}=\begin{pmatrix}0&*\\G_{n-2,p-1}&*\end{pmatrix}$ and $G^{22}_{n,p}=\begin{pmatrix}\delta G_{n-2,p-1}&*\\ *&*\end{pmatrix}$: the type-1/type-3 pairing has unmatched defects and is zero, cutting a type-2/type-3 terminal arc leaves the same exterior matching, and a type-3/type-3 pairing creates one loop. Let $A=G_{n-2,p}$, $B=G_{n-2,p-1}$, and write the rank-$(n-1)$ form as $G_{n-1,p}=\begin{pmatrix}A&AV_0\\V_0^{\mathsf T}A&V_0^{\mathsf T}AV_0+\alpha_{n-1,p}B\end{pmatrix}$; at $n=2p+1$ the $A,V_0$ blocks are empty and their products are omitted. If $V=\begin{pmatrix}V^{11}&*\\V^{21}&*\end{pmatrix}$ is the off-diagonal block in the orthogonalizing basis change of step 3.1, then $G^{12}_{n,p}=G_{n-1,p}V$ gives $0=AV^{11}+AV_0V^{21}$ and $B=V_0^{\mathsf T}AV^{11}+(V_0^{\mathsf T}AV_0+\alpha_{n-1,p}B)V^{21}$. The induction hypothesis makes $A$ invertible when nonempty, so the first equation gives $V^{11}=-V_0V^{21}$; at $n=2p+1$ these blocks are omitted. Substitution in the second equation cancels the $A$-terms and yields $B=\alpha_{n-1,p}BV^{21}$. The induction hypothesis makes $B$ invertible for generic $q$, so multiplication by $B^{-1}$ gives $I=\alpha_{n-1,p}V^{21}$ and hence $\alpha_{n-1,p}\ne0$ and $V^{21}=\alpha_{n-1,p}^{-1}I$.

The top-left block of $G^{22}_{n,p}=V^{\mathsf T}G_{n-1,p}V+\alpha_{n,p}G_{n-1,p-1}$ is $\delta B$. Its first term is $(V^{11})^{\mathsf T}AV^{11}+(V^{11})^{\mathsf T}AV_0V^{21}+(V^{21})^{\mathsf T}V_0^{\mathsf T}AV^{11}+(V^{21})^{\mathsf T}(V_0^{\mathsf T}AV_0+\alpha_{n-1,p}B)V^{21}$. Substituting $V^{11}=-V_0V^{21}$ makes the coefficients of $(V^{21})^{\mathsf T}V_0^{\mathsf T}AV_0V^{21}$ equal $1-1-1+1=0$ and leaves $\alpha_{n-1,p}(V^{21})^{\mathsf T}BV^{21}=\alpha_{n-1,p}^{-1}B$. The first block of $G_{n-1,p-1}$ is $B$, so cancelling invertible $B$ gives $\alpha_{n,p}=\delta-1/\alpha_{n-1,p}$.

The quantum-integer recurrence [F5] solves this scalar recurrence as $\alpha_{n,p}=[n-2p+2]_q/[n-2p+1]_q$: the boundary value at $n=2p$ is $[2]_q/[1]_q=\delta$, and if $\alpha_{n-1,p}=[n-2p+1]_q/[n-2p]_q$, then $\delta-1/\alpha_{n-1,p}=\delta-[n-2p]_q/[n-2p+1]_q=[n-2p+2]_q/[n-2p+1]_q$.

The determinant of the orthogonal block form in step 3.1 and its unit-determinant basis change gives $\det G_{n,p}=([n-2p+2]_q/[n-2p+1]_q)^{d_{n-1,p-1}}\det G_{n-1,p}\det G_{n-1,p-1}$ for $n>2p$, while step 3.2 gives $\det G_{2p,p}=\delta^{d_{2p-1,p-1}}\det G_{2p-1,p-1}$; also $\det G_{n,0}=1$ by step 2.1.

Let $P_{n,p}=\prod_{j=1}^p([n-2p+1+j]_q/[j]_q)^{d_{n,p-j}}$. For $n>2p$, put $h=n-2p+1$. If $p=1$, $P_{n,1}=([h+1]/[h])P_{n-1,1}$. If $p\ge2$, the numerator $[h+j]$ for $2\le j<p$ receives exponents $d_{n-1,p-j-1}$ and $d_{n-1,p-j}$ from the two lower-rank products, summing to $d_{n,p-j}$; at $j=1$ the missing exponent is supplied by $([h+1]/[h])^{d_{n-1,p-1}}$, whose denominator cancels the extra $[h]$, and at $j=p$ the second lower-rank product supplies exponent $d_{n,0}=1$. The denominator exponents add as $d_{n-1,p-j}+d_{n-1,p-j-1}=d_{n,p-j}$ (with the endpoint $j=p$ supplied by the first lower-rank product). Thus $P_{n,p}$ satisfies the recurrence in step 7.1 by Pascal's identity for $d_{n,r}$.

At $n=2p$, $P_{2,1}=[2]=\delta$ for $p=1$. For $p\ge2$, compare net exponents of each quantum integer in $P_{2p,p}$ and $[2]^{d_{2p-1,p-1}}P_{2p-1,p-1}$: for $2\le m\le p$ the exponent is $d_{2p,p-m+1}-d_{2p,p-m}=d_{2p-1,p-m+1}-d_{2p-1,p-m-1}$ by Pascal's identity, exactly the exponent supplied by the latter product; for $m=p+1$ both exponents are $d_{2p,0}=d_{2p-1,0}=1$, and $[1]=1$. Hence $P_{2p,p}=\delta^{d_{2p-1,p-1}}P_{2p-1,p-1}$, the boundary recurrence in step 7.1.

Induction using steps 7.1–8.2 now gives $\det G_{n,p}=P_{n,p}$ for every $q^2$ not a root of unity. Every Gram entry is polynomial in $\delta$, so its determinant is polynomial; the displayed product is rational in $q$ and agrees with that determinant on the infinite set where $q^2$ is not a root of unity. After putting the difference over a common denominator, its polynomial numerator has infinitely many zeros and is identically zero. Thus each displayed zero-over-zero value has the unique removable continuation given by the Gram determinant, proving the formula for every $q\in\mathbb C^\times$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a
finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$,
where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict
order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For
$\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned
by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$.

Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular
algebra**, if:

(i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$
for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$
and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite
algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and

(ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$
there exist coefficients $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$), independent of $s$, such that for every $s\in T(\lambda)$
$$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free
$R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$;
condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by
$c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when
$c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and
it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$, the left action being
$a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_t\,i(a)$. Both actions are well defined on
the freely spanning basis elements by (ii): the coefficients $r_v$ are unique
because $C$ is an $R$-basis of $A$ and the quotient by $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ kills
exactly the basis elements indexed by strictly larger labels, while applying
the anti-automorphism (i) to (ii) gives the same triangularity for left
multiplication. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of
$\lambda$, and
$$A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$$
via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$,
where $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ is spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with
$\mu\unrhd\lambda$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.

derivations.claim: Write $d_t=\dim_{\mathbb C}W_{n,t}$. By [F1] and [F3], $\dim\mathrm{TL}_n=\sum_t d_t^2$. By [F2], each simple module is exactly one $D_{n,t}$ with nonzero form quotient, and these modules are pairwise nonisomorphic. If $\phi_{n,t}$ is degenerate then either it is identically zero, so $\dim D_{n,t}=0<d_t$, or its radical is nonzero, so again $\dim D_{n,t}<d_t$.

Suppose $\mathrm{TL}_n$ is semisimple. By [F4] and [F6], each division algebra factor $D_i$ is finite-dimensional over the central copy of $\mathbb C$. For $x\in D_i$, left multiplication by $x$ has a complex eigenvalue $\lambda$, and a nonzero eigenvector gives $(x-\lambda)y=0$, which forces $x=\lambda$ in a division algebra. Thus $D_i=\mathbb C$, the right simple module for the factor $M_{m_i}(D_i)$ has dimension $m_i$, and the right regular module contains $m_i$ copies of it. Consequently $\dim\mathrm{TL}_n$ is the sum of the squares of the dimensions of its pairwise nonisomorphic simple right modules. By [F2], these are the $D_{n,t}$. If any form were degenerate, step 1.1 would make this sum strictly smaller than $\sum_t d_t^2=\dim\mathrm{TL}_n$, a contradiction. Thus all forms are nondegenerate.

Conversely suppose every form is nondegenerate. Then [F2] gives $D_{n,t}=W_{n,t}\ne0$ for every allowed $t$, so these are the complete simple right-module list and [F3] says that the squares of their dimensions sum to $\dim\mathrm{TL}_n$. By [F5], the quotient by the Jacobson radical is semisimple, and its simple right modules are exactly those of $\mathrm{TL}_n$ because the radical annihilates every simple right module. In particular, this quotient is nonzero. Applying the right-module dimension formula from step 2.1 to it shows that its dimension is the sum of the squares of those same simple dimensions. Therefore the quotient has the same dimension as $\mathrm{TL}_n$, the radical has dimension zero, and $\mathrm{TL}_n$ is semisimple.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and let $\delta\in R$. The object labels are the nonnegative integers $n=0,1,2,\ldots$. For labels $m,n$, place bottom points $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ and top points $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ along the rectangle from left to right on their respective edges. Their cyclic order is $t_1,\ldots,t_n,b_m,\ldots,b_1$. When $m=n=0$, the empty matching is included.

An $(m,n)$ **diagram** is a perfect matching of these $m+n$ boundary labels which is noncrossing: there are no four labels $a,b,c,d$ in cyclic order whose matched pairs are $\{a,c\}$ and $\{b,d\}$. A picture consists of disjoint arcs realizing the matching; equality is equality of the matching, so planar deformation that fixes the boundary does not change a diagram. If $m+n$ is odd, there are no such diagrams. Write $\mathcal D(m,n)$ for this set and define the $R$-module

$$M_R(m,n):=R^{(\mathcal D(m,n))},$$

the free $R$-module on the set of diagrams ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]). In particular, its diagram basis is empty when $m+n$ is odd.

For basis diagrams $D:m\to n$ and $E:n\to p$, stack $E$ above $D$ and identify the $n$ matching boundary points. The resulting finite graph has degree two at each identified point, where degree means the number of incident arcs. Each component is a path joining two exterior boundary points or a closed cycle. Remove every cycle and multiply the remaining exterior matching by $\delta^c$, where $c$ is the number of removed cycles. Denote this output by $E\circ D$ and extend the rule $R$-bilinearly to a map $M_R(n,p)\times M_R(m,n)\to M_R(m,p)$. A following result proves closure of these operations on the diagram modules and the category axioms.

The matching $1_n:n\to n$ pairs each bottom point to the top point directly above it. Horizontal juxtaposition, with the left diagram placed first, defines $m\otimes m'=m+m'$ on object labels and $D\otimes D'$ on basis diagrams; extend it $R$-bilinearly to the modules. A following result proves that these operations give a strict monoidal category.

For $1\le i<n$, let $d_i\in M_R(n,n)$ be the diagram with a cap joining top points $i,i+1$, a cup joining bottom points $i,i+1$, and vertical through strands at every other position. Define $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ to be the $R$-module $M_R(n,n)$ with bilinear multiplication $xy:=x\circ y$ and distinguished element $1_n$. A following result proves that it is a unital associative $R$-algebra and identifies it with the endomorphism algebra at object $n$.

The left factor is stacked above the right factor. The loop value is $\delta$; no invertibility or nonzero condition on $\delta$ is part of these data.

For every commutative ring $R$, loop value $\delta\in R$, and objects $m,n,p,q\ge0$, the raw diagram data of [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]] form a strict monoidal category $\mathcal{TL}_R(\delta)$ with hom-modules $M_R(m,n)$ and the stated $R$-bilinear stacking composition. Composition is associative, the identity diagrams are two-sided identities, and horizontal juxtaposition is a strict monoidal bifunctor with unit object $0$. Consequently $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{TL}_R(\delta)}(n)=\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ is a unital associative $R$-algebra whose underlying $R$-module is free on its noncrossing pairing diagrams.

For every $n\ge0$, each basis diagram in $\mathcal D(n,n)$ is a finite product of the elementary diagrams $d_1,\ldots,d_{n-1}$ from [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]]. The product can be chosen so that no intermediate stack creates a closed cycle. Therefore the set of diagrams lies in the unital subalgebra of $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ generated by these diagrams.

For a unital ring $R$ and a set $X$, the **free left $R$-module on $X$** is
$$R^{(X)}:=\bigoplus_{x\in X}R.$$
For $x\in X$, the **standard basis vector** $e_x$ has coordinate $1_R$ at $x$ and zero elsewhere. Every element is represented by a unique finitely supported coefficient family $(r_x)_{x\in X}$, and is written
$$\sum_{x\in X}r_xe_x.$$
The **standard basis map** $X\to R^{(X)}$ sends $x$ to $e_x$. It is injective exactly when $1_R\ne0$ or $X$ has at most one element; in these cases it is the standard basis inclusion. Indeed, for distinct $x,y$ the $x$-coordinates of $e_x$ and $e_y$ are $1_R$ and $0$. For the zero ring every $e_x$ is zero, but the indexed family $(e_x)_{x\in X}$ still has unique finitely supported coefficients.

More generally, a family $(b_x)_{x\in X}$ is a **basis** of a module $M$ when every element of $M$ is uniquely a finite $R$-linear combination of the $b_x$ ([[def-generated-cyclic-finitely-generated-and-free-modules]]). For $X=\varnothing$, $R^{(X)}=0$ and its empty family is a basis.
